by: Claude Code (opus), titles and abstracts only

question.population: Adults, including smokers, former smokers and people exposed to asbestos
question.intervention: Beta-carotene supplements (alone or with other vitamins)

decisions.reason: Pools RCTs of beta-carotene supplements and lung cancer risk in people without lung cancer, with a subgroup for smokers and asbestos workers.
Pools randomised trials of beta-carotene supplements and lung cancer incidence in current and former smokers, which is within the target population.
Pools six RCTs comparing beta-carotene supplements with placebo for lung cancer risk; the observational studies are analysed separately.

question.population: Adults, healthy or with various diseases
question.intervention: Beta-carotene or vitamin A supplements (alone or with other antioxidants, with results for them apart)

decisions.reason: Pooled RCTs in adults with any health condition comparing beta-carotene with placebo or no intervention on death from any cause.
Pooled RCTs of vitamin A versus control on mortality, but the population is children under 5, not adults.
Pooled RCTs in adults giving separate all-cause mortality results for beta-carotene and vitamin A versus placebo or no intervention.
Pooled placebo-controlled RCTs of vitamin A given to postpartum mothers, but the outcome is infant death, not the adults' own death.
Pooled RCTs in healthy adults and adults with diseases testing antioxidants including beta-carotene and vitamin A versus placebo on mortality.
Pooled RCTs in adults versus placebo or no intervention, with separate all-cause mortality results for vitamin A and beta-carotene.
Pooled RCTs in adults versus placebo or no intervention, reporting all-cause mortality separately for beta-carotene and vitamin A.
A narrative critical review of Indian trials in children with no pooled analysis; both the population and the method differ.
Protocol for adult primary-prevention trials of supplements incl. beta-carotene/vitamin A vs control on all-cause mortality, but no pooled results yet.
Re-examines antioxidant trials (beta-carotene, vitamin A, E) in adults, but tallies trials' primary outcomes rather than pooling all-cause mortality.
A comment on a review of maternal postpartum vitamin A for infant mortality, so the population and outcome differ.

question.population: Adults in general or older adults (not a group defined by one illness, such as people in intensive care, on dialysis or with cancer)
question.intervention: Beta-carotene supplements (alone or with other vitamins)

decisions.reason: Pooled only case-control and cohort studies of carotenoid intake; it did not pool randomised trials of beta-carotene supplements.
Pooled RCTs of beta-carotene supplements in people without lung cancer and reported lung cancer incidence.
Studied breast cancer survivors taking vitamins A, C or E after diagnosis; the outcome was survival, not new cancers.
Pooled RCTs in healthy adults of beta-carotene, with or without vitamin A, and reported lung cancer incidence.
Pooled beta-carotene RCTs for lung cancer, but reported results only for current and former smokers, a narrower group.
Pooled RCTs of beta-carotene alone versus placebo for cancer incidence, with a separate primary prevention analysis.
Pooled RCTs of supplements for bladder cancer, with a subgroup for beta-carotene alone.
Pooled RCTs of beta-carotene versus placebo for overall cancer incidence and incidence by cancer site.
Pooled beta-carotene with other antioxidants, including selenium, for gastrointestinal cancers; no beta-carotene-only cancer result is reported.
Pooled six RCTs of beta-carotene supplements versus placebo for lung cancer risk.
Pooled RCTs of beta-carotene versus placebo for prostate cancer incidence.
Pooled beta-carotene with other antioxidants, including selenium, for gastrointestinal cancers; beta-carotene-specific results cover mortality only.
Pooled beta-carotene with other antioxidants, including selenium, for gastrointestinal cancers; no beta-carotene-only cancer result is reported.
Pooled beta-carotene with other antioxidants, including selenium, for gastrointestinal cancers; beta-carotene-specific results cover mortality only.
In general adults, beta-carotene was given only with minerals such as selenium and zinc, and the trials were summarised without pooling.
Plans to pool primary-prevention trials in adults that include beta-carotene, with cancer incidence as an outcome, but this is only a protocol with no pooled results yet.

question.intervention: Preformed vitamin A (retinol) supplements in early pregnancy

decisions.reason: Looks at maternal vitamin A, C or E intake, mostly in observational studies, and child breathing problems, not birth defects; vitamin A was not pooled.
Pooled RCTs of vitamin A in pregnancy or breastfeeding, but outcomes are only nutrient blood levels, not birth defects.
Looks at retinol in breast milk and postpartum supplements, not supplements in early pregnancy or birth defects.
Covers vitamin A in pregnancy and reports birth defects, but that result comes from observational studies of vitamin A given with other nutrients.
Pooled RCTs of vitamin A alone vs placebo in pregnant women, but the abstract reports mortality, preterm birth and birthweight, not birth defects.
Looks at vitamin A for preventing or treating malaria in pregnancy and childhood, not birth defects.
Pooled RCTs of vitamin A in pregnant women, but the abstract reports mortality, anaemia, infection and birthweight, not birth defects.
Withdrawn review of vitamin A RCTs in pregnancy; it did no pooling and reports maternal outcomes, not birth defects.
Looks at supplements given to mothers after birth and infant deaths or illness, not early pregnancy or birth defects.
Reviews vitamin A RCTs in pregnant women, but it did no pooling and reports maternal outcomes, not birth defects.
Pooled trials of vitamin A or beta-carotene in pregnancy, but the abstract reports birthweight, fetal loss and mortality, not birth defects.
This is a comment on a review of postpartum vitamin A for infant death and illness, not early-pregnancy supplements and birth defects.

question.population: Children aged 6 months to 5 years, mostly in low- and middle-income countries

decisions.reason: Vitamin A is used to treat children who already have pneumonia, and the review mainly compares doses with each other rather than with placebo.
Vitamin A vs control to prevent infection in LMIC children, but ages run up to 7 years, neonates are included, and the only outcome is upper respiratory infections.
This reviews food-based approaches, not supplements, in women and children, with vitamin A status as the outcome.
The population is very-low-birth-weight preterm infants and the outcomes are neonatal conditions such as BPD, a different question.
Vitamin A in malnourished LMIC children, but it is mixed with other nutrients, non-randomised studies are included, and the outcome is only vaccine seroconversion.
Randomised trials of vitamin A alone vs placebo in children, but the only outcome is respiratory infection and the age range is not stated.
This covers beta-carotene supplements in adults, a different intervention and population.
Pools randomised trials of vitamin A supplements in community children aged 6 months to 5 years for death and illness.
Vitamin A is given to mothers during pregnancy and the outcomes are fetal and newborn growth.
Updated meta-analysis of randomised trials of vitamin A supplements vs control for death in children under five in LMICs.
Pools randomised trials of vitamin A supplements in community children aged 6 months to 5 years for death and illness.
Meta-analysis of randomised trials of vitamin A vs control for death in children under five in vitamin A deficient countries.
Vitamin A vs placebo is given to treat children who already have measles, and the outcomes are blindness and blood retinol.
Pools randomised trials of vitamin A supplements in children aged 6 months to 5 years for death, diarrhoea and measles.
Vitamin A is an add-on treatment for children who already have pneumonia, not prevention in healthy children.
Vitamin A vs placebo is given to treat children who already have measles, and the outcomes are blindness and blood retinol.
This reviews micronutrient-fortified foods, not vitamin A supplements, with growth and blood markers as outcomes.
Vitamin A vs placebo is given to treat children who already have measles, and the outcomes are blindness and blood retinol.
Vitamin A vs placebo for death and illness in LMICs, but the children are infants aged 6 months or younger, or their mothers after birth.
Pools randomised trials of vitamin A supplements in community children aged 6 months to 5 years for death and illness.
Vitamin A vs placebo or no supplementation with death as an outcome, but the population is very low birth weight newborns, not children 6 months to 5 years.
Pooled randomised trials of vitamin A supplements in children 6 months to 7 years, with diarrhoea and respiratory infection outcomes.
Trials of antioxidant supplements in adults aged 18 to 103, not young children.
School-age children; looks at helminths with micronutrient status and multimicronutrient effects on worm infection, not vitamin A for death or illness.
Vitamin A vs control with death as an outcome, but the population is very low birth weight newborns, not children 6 months to 5 years.
Vitamin A to prevent lower respiratory infections in children up to 7, but results are described trial by trial with no pooled estimate.
Placebo-controlled trials on infant death and illness, but the vitamin A was given to mothers after birth, not to the children.
Vitamin A for death and morbidity, but in very low birth weight newborns compared with standard vitamin A regimens.
Antioxidant supplements for preventing death in adults, not young children.
Antioxidant prevention trials in healthy people and patients with mostly adult diseases, not young children.
Vitamin A in children, but for treating severe acute malnutrition, mainly comparing high and low doses, with no pooled analysis.
Antioxidant supplement trials in adults, not young children.
Pooled controlled trials of vitamin A supplements given to children in communities, with child death as the outcome.
Vitamin A trials on child death and illness, but limited to India and appraised narratively without pooling.
Vitamin A vs placebo for death and complications, but it treats children who already have measles rather than preventing illness.
Includes vitamin A supplement trials in children, but the outcome is linear growth, not death or illness.
Vitamin A in children, but as an added treatment for existing non-measles pneumonia rather than prevention.
Vitamin A for death and morbidity, but in very low birth weight newborns compared with standard vitamin A regimens.
Vitamin A vs placebo for death in children 6 months to 13 years, but it treats existing measles rather than preventing illness.
Vitamin A for death and morbidity, but in very low birth weight newborns compared with standard vitamin A regimens.
Vitamin A vs placebo in children with death and complications as outcomes, but it treats diagnosed measles rather than preventing illness.
Vitamin A vs placebo in children with death and complications as outcomes, but it treats diagnosed measles rather than preventing illness.
Vitamin A trials in children aged 0-5 in low- and middle-income countries match, but the outcome is growth, not death or illness.
This is a protocol covering many supplements in adults, with chronic disease and death outcomes, not young children.
Re-examines antioxidant trials in mixed, mostly adult groups by primary outcome, rather than vitamin A in young children.
A comment on a review of vitamin A given to mothers after birth, not to children aged 6 months to 5 years.
